lesson.subtitle: Lesson 31 -- Conference Introduction and Elevator Pitch
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Eduarda | Lesson 31 -- Conference Introduction and Elevator Pitch

listenings.text: Hi Eduarda, it's James. Congratulations again on the committee. Now, the forum in New York. The keynote is on Thursday at nine, and your breakout session is at two in the afternoon. The room is small, about forty people, so it's a great chance to meet investors. Please prepare a thirty-second pitch for the coffee breaks. Don't start with your job title. Start with a hook, something that people remember. And bring business cards. Last year the forum was so busy that I ran out of cards before lunch. Have a good flight.

Most people at a conference introduce themselves in the same way: name, company and job title. Then they wonder why nobody remembers them. A good elevator pitch has three parts. First, a hook: one sentence about the problem that you solve. Second, proof: a short example with a number, so that people believe you. Third, a question that opens the conversation. Keep it under thirty seconds. And practice it so many times that it sounds natural, not memorized. Your expertise is important, but people remember stories, not titles.

extra_audio.text: James left Eduarda a voicemail about the forum in New York. On the plane, she wrote a thirty-second pitch. On Thursday morning, she listened to the keynote. At the coffee break, she met Nathan Cole from Bluewater Capital. She told him about a case that was so complex that they negotiated with forty creditors. In the afternoon, Nathan came to her breakout session.
